newsitem.title: GERMANY: Few chances seen for compromise in Bonn-Buba clash.
newsitem.headline: Few chances seen for compromise in Bonn-Buba clash.

text.p: The Bundesbank and Bonn are searching for a face-saving compromise to their clash over the revaluation of the central bank's reserves but economists said on Friday there appeared no clear way out for either side.
The fight will likely end with Bonn using political clout to get the funds despite strong public criticism and calls from opposition parties for Finance Minister Theo Waigel to quit.

It may also shore up the confidence of other European nation using unorthodox measures to meet Maastricht Treaty entry criteria to join European monetary union (EMU) at the start in January 1999, which Germany had often chastised.

Escalating tensions may prompt the Bundesbank to curb support for the currency -- and possibly try to delay or derail EMU amid fears the euro will be too weak -- since the central bank has long stressed the criteria must be met credibily.

"The Bundesbank does not make the EMU decision. But if the Bundesbank does not support EMU, the EMU proposal will die a little death as soon as it reaches parliament," said Alison Cottrell, chief international economist at PaineWebber.
"If Germany finds it harder to meet the letter of the criteria, this makes EMU less likely - not a broad EMU more likely," said Cottrell from PaineWebber's London office.
Waigel has said the funds he has asked to receive this year would be welcome but not essential to meet EMU entry criteria.

But the request was poor timing and the fact Waigel wants an actual transfer of book profits prompted the Bundesbank's public fight since the transfer would effectively heat up money supply growth and in turn inflationary pressures.

Some independent economists agree with Waigel's outlook, saying Germany's higher growth rate for 1997 and lower costs still give Bonn a fighting chance to meet the 3.0 percent deficit hurdle to enter currency union.
Others, however, say Waigel needs to find all the money he can since it was now too early to judge for sure whether Germany could make the grade without any one-off measures.
But Waigel's plan to put the funds against long-term debt would also help his deficit fight by freeing up funds otherwise earmarked to pay off the debt and for interest payments.

They also say the Bundesbank is worried Waigel may change his mind and seek European Union approval to put the funds directly against Bonn's deficit, arguing previous Bundesbank transfers to Bonn to help cut the deficit have set precedent.

"If the payout is not for deficit reduction, I really wonder why Waigel is so keen to get the money if he is so sure of getting close to the deficit criteria," said Hermann Remsperger, chief economist at BHF-Bank in Frankfurt.
Waigel faces the precarious position of seeking to meet the deficit criteria in the treaty that forces him to be at 3.0 percent or less of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 1997.
The Bundesbank has offered little help with its stance against Bonn's intentions to go to parliament in early June to seek approval for the funds transfer.

Neither have Germany's opposition parties who are against more spending cuts or Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partner Free Democrats, who undermined Waigel's recent proposal to raise the gasoline tax to plug the deficit hole.
"Waigel cannot hope to show up with a deficit at 3.4 percent and still hope to make it in," said one senior economist at a major international bank. "It just won't work."

Instead, the Bundesbank will not give up its public fight against the transfer of funds in 1997, even though its strong statement on Wednesday that set off the feud stated the bank may consider transfer payments once the union starts in 1999.
Some economists still see a chance for compromise between Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer.

"On principle, Bonn will win but the actual implementation will have some concessions in the end," said Thomas Mayer, chief economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt. "Both sides will go to great pains to say currency union will take place."
Mayer, however, said he does not think Germany can get to the 3.0 percent deficit level without the Bundesbank transfer.

"I think in the rest of 1997 Germany will have to move toward a more flexible interpretation of the deficit criteria. They will basically converge with France, which seems to me also on the way to a more flexible interpretation," Mayer said.
